history.content:
If you have the cash to purchase a car outright, doing so will save you the most money—essentially choosing a 0-month payment plan. The cash for the car should be readily accessible; Additionally, you should avoid becoming "cash-poor" by using all your savings for the car purchase.
If cash isn't an option, the best approach is to select the longest loan period that offers a favorable interest rate. This option allows you to lock in a lower rate for an extended time, which helps keep your minimum monthly payments as low as possible. Additionally, a lower rate means you save on interest. Remember, you can generally pay off the loan sooner by making extra or larger payments.
As for leasing, it's advisable to avoid it unless you can write off the monthly lease payments as a business expense. If you are weighing monthly lease payments against depreciation for tax purposes, leasing can sometimes be the more sensible choice.

A lease is essentially a rental agreement. When you lease a vehicle, you borrow money to cover the expected depreciation of the car over the lease term. Your monthly payment is calculated based on the sale price minus the residual value. Generally, leasing tends to cost more over time compared to outright ownership. Leasing a vehicle involves making monthly payments for the right to use the car for a specific duration. At the end of the lease, you typically have the option to return the vehicle, purchase it, or lease a different one.
When is it convenient to lease?

In two situations, leasing a car can make sense. First, leasing is the right choice if you prefer to drive a new vehicle every 2 to 3 years. However, keep in mind that if you exceed the allowed mileage, you’ll incur additional charges at the end of the lease.
Second, if you can deduct the monthly lease payments as a business expense, leasing can also be beneficial. It’s particularly advantageous if you anticipate earning more money in the future, allowing you the option to upgrade to a new car later on.
How much do I need to put down for the down payment?

evidence.text: ponents. Experts say life insurance, a will, a living will and a durable power of attorney are all important aspects of an estate plan that should be established at the start of the planning process. In the event of an untimely death, life insurance can replace lost earnings, which can be especially beneficial for younger individuals, says Bill Kirchick, a partner with Bingham McCutchen law firm in Boston. ""Young people can't afford to die,"" he says. ""They are going to lose a source of income if something happens to a young couple and they haven't had enough time to accumulate wealth from earnings to put aside in savings or a retirement plan."" Also, the earlier you take out a life insurance policy, the more likely you are to be approved for reduced rates compared to older individuals. Utilize estate planning professionals.

If you don't know how to evaluate funds and are looking for someone to help you make good investment decisions, then you want a financial advisor.  My suggestion is to look for one that 1) doesn't try to sell you insurance first (since insurance is an expense, not an investment), 2) can explain to you the the relationship between risk and return (and what mix is right for you) and 3) recommends funds that have good demonstrated returns after fees have been removed. If you plan to pick your own funds and just want a transaction broker, go with one of the free/cheap online discount brokers.

Generally speaking, you're better served by an advisor who collects an annual fee based on a percentage of your account value. Advisors who are compensated based on transactions have a vested interest to churn your account, which is often not in your best interest. You also need to be wary of advisors who peddle expensive mutual funds with sales loads (aka kick-backs to the advisor) or annuities. Your advisor's compensation structure should be transparent as well.
